question: How does a large language model work, just enough to evaluate one?

scenes.sub: Tokens in, probabilities out, one token at a time.
scenes.say: How an L L M works, just enough to evaluate one. You don't need the math. You need the right mental model.

scenes.head: Think of your phone keyboard
scenes.say: Start with something you already use. On your phone keyboard, you type, see you, and it suggests tomorrow, soon, or later. It is guessing the next word from patterns. A large language model, or L L M, is that same autocomplete, trained on a huge amount of text and run again and again, one piece at a time.

scenes.head: The loop behind every answer
scenes.say: A model never sees words. Your text is chopped into tokens, small pieces of words. The model reads those tokens and gives a probability to every possible next token. Then one token is picked, added to the text, and the whole loop repeats until the answer is done.

scenes.head: Next-token prediction

panels.code:
Prompt so far:
"The capital of France is"

The model scores every token
in its vocabulary. We turn the
scores into probabilities and
pick one.

scenes.say: Say the prompt is, the capital of France is. The model gives every token a score, and the scores become probabilities. Paris gets ninety two percent. A few others share a little. These numbers are illustrative, but the shape is real: a few likely tokens, then a long tail. Always taking the top one is called greedy decoding.

scenes.head: Temperature reshapes the odds
scenes.say: Temperature controls how that list is used. Low temperature sharpens it, so the top token wins almost every time. Answers are steady. High temperature flattens it, so unlikely tokens get picked more often. Answers get varied, and riskier. At temperature zero, you get nearly the same answer every run.

scenes.head: Why evaluators sample more than once

panels.code:
Prompt: What is 17 times 6?

run 1: 102   correct
run 2: 102   correct
run 3: 112   wrong
run 4: 102   correct
run 5: 96    wrong

scenes.say: Here is why this matters when you grade. One run is one sample. The model may be right once and wrong the next time. So run the same prompt several times and judge the pattern. Three out of five is a very different story from five out of five. If asked why the same prompt gives different answers, the answer is sampling.

scenes.head: In the interview
rows: Why does the same prompt vary?
A word piece, about four letters
Calling the model a database of facts
It predicts text, it does not look facts up
scenes.say: Likely follow-ups. Why does the same prompt vary? It samples from probabilities. Is temperature zero fully fixed? Nearly, but not guaranteed. What is a token? A word piece, roughly four letters of English. The common mistake is calling the model a database of facts. It predicts text, it does not look facts up.

lines: An L L M predicts one token at a time from a probability list.
Temperature flattens or sharpens that list.
Output is a sample, so judge patterns over several runs.
scenes.say: An L L M predicts the next token from a list of probabilities, one token at a time. Temperature sharpens or flattens that list. And because output is a sample, judge patterns over several runs, not one lucky answer.
